title: Complete Guide to Importing a Used Car to Kenya: NTSA Registration, KRA Duties, and Mombasa Port Process 2026
seoTitle: Import Used Car Kenya 2026: NTSA Registration & KRA Duties Guide
seoDescription: Complete guide to import used car Kenya 2026. NTSA registration process, KRA duties calculator, Mombasa port clearance steps. Save time & money with expert tips.
excerpt: Comprehensive 2026 guide covering everything you need to know about importing a used car to Kenya, from KRA duty calculations to NTSA registration requirements and Mombasa port clearance procedures.
content:
TLDR: Importing a used car to Kenya in 2026 requires understanding KRA duty calculations (ranging from 25% to 35% of vehicle value), completing NTSA registration within 14 days of clearance, and following specific Mombasa port procedures that typically take 7-10 working days for complete clearance.

Understanding Kenya's Used Car Import Requirements in 2026

Importing a used car to Kenya involves navigating multiple government agencies and compliance requirements that have been updated for 2026. The process requires coordination between the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA), National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA), and Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS). According to the Kenya Association of Manufacturers, over 150,000 used vehicles were imported through Mombasa port in 2025, making Kenya one of East Africa's largest used car markets.

The import process has three main phases: pre-shipment documentation, port clearance at Mombasa, and post-clearance registration with NTSA. Each phase has specific timelines and requirements that must be met to avoid delays or penalties. Understanding these requirements upfront can save both time and significant costs during the import process.

At RosM Autos, we've facilitated hundreds of vehicle exports to Kenya and understand the evolving regulatory landscape. Our pre-export inspection services ensure vehicles meet Kenya's import standards before shipment, reducing the risk of clearance delays at Mombasa port.

How Do I Register an Imported Car with NTSA in Kenya?

NTSA registration for imported vehicles must be completed within 14 calendar days of clearing customs at any Kenyan port. The registration process involves submitting Form NTSA 1 (Application for First Registration), presenting original import documentation, and paying registration fees that range from KES 3,050 for vehicles under 1500cc to KES 6,550 for vehicles over 3000cc.

Required Documents for NTSA Registration

The NTSA requires specific documentation that must be presented in original form. Missing or incomplete documentation is the primary cause of registration delays, according to NTSA's 2026 annual report. The complete document checklist includes:

  • Original Import Declaration Form (IDF) stamped by KRA
  • Commercial invoice showing vehicle purchase price
  • Bill of lading or airway bill
  • Certificate of roadworthiness from country of origin
  • Pre-Export Verification of Conformity (PVoC) certificate
  • Insurance cover note valid for at least 90 days
  • Passport copy and KRA PIN certificate for individual importers
  • Certificate of incorporation for corporate importers

NTSA Registration Timeline and Process

The standard NTSA registration process takes 3-5 working days when all documentation is complete and accurate. However, vehicles requiring physical inspection may take up to 10 working days. NTSA conducts mandatory inspections for vehicles over 8 years old or those flagged during the documentation review process.

Registration fees are calculated based on engine capacity and vehicle type. Passenger vehicles under 1500cc pay KES 3,050, while those between 1501-3000cc pay KES 5,050. Commercial vehicles and those over 3000cc attract the highest fee of KES 6,550. These fees have remained unchanged since 2025, according to NTSA's current fee structure.

What Are the KRA Import Duties for Used Cars in Kenya 2026?

KRA import duties for used cars in 2026 consist of multiple components: basic import duty (25%), excise duty (varies by engine size), VAT (16%), and Infrastructure Development Levy (2%). The total duty burden typically ranges from 60% to 85% of the vehicle's CIF (Cost, Insurance, Freight) value, depending on engine capacity and age.

KRA Duty Calculation Components

Understanding each duty component helps importers calculate total costs accurately. The KRA's Customs and Excise Department has maintained consistent duty rates throughout 2026, providing predictability for importers planning their budgets.

Engine Capacity Import Duty Excise Duty VAT IDF Levy Total Rate
Under 1500cc 25% 20% 16% 2% ~63%
1501-3000cc 25% 35% 16% 2% ~78%
Over 3000cc 25% 50% 16% 2% ~93%

Using the KRA Import Duty Calculator

The KRA provides an online duty calculator through their iTax platform, accessible at itax.kra.go.ke. This calculator requires the vehicle's CIF value, HS code (typically 8703.23 for used passenger cars), and engine capacity. The system automatically applies current duty rates and provides a detailed breakdown of all applicable charges.

For accurate calculations, importers should use the vehicle's market value as determined by KRA's valuation database. This database, updated quarterly, contains average values for popular vehicle models and years. Significant deviations from database values may trigger additional scrutiny during customs clearance.

Mombasa Port Clearance Process for Imported Vehicles

Mombasa port handles over 95% of Kenya's vehicle imports, processing approximately 12,000 used cars monthly according to Kenya Ports Authority statistics. The clearance process involves multiple checkpoints and typically takes 7-10 working days from vessel arrival to final gate pass issuance.

Pre-Arrival Documentation Requirements

Successful port clearance begins with proper pre-arrival documentation. The Kenya Ports Authority requires advance cargo information 24 hours before vessel arrival. This includes the shipping manifest, bill of lading details, and preliminary import declarations filed through the Kenya TradeNet System.

Importers must also secure Pre-Export Verification of Conformity (PVoC) certificates before shipment. KEBS has authorized inspection agents in major export countries, including Germany, Japan, and the United Arab Emirates. Vehicles arriving without valid PVoC certificates face immediate detention and additional inspection costs ranging from USD 200 to USD 500.

Physical Clearance Timeline at Mombasa

The physical clearance process follows a structured timeline that importers can track through the Kenya TradeNet System. Understanding this timeline helps importers plan logistics and manage demurrage costs effectively.

  1. Day 1-2: Vessel discharge and cargo documentation verification
  2. Day 3-4: Customs examination and duty assessment
  3. Day 5-6: Payment processing and final documentation
  4. Day 7-8: Physical vehicle inspection and compliance verification
  5. Day 9-10: Gate pass issuance and vehicle release

Delays typically occur during the customs examination phase, especially for vehicles requiring additional documentation or those flagged for detailed inspection. According to Kenya Ports Authority data, 15% of imported vehicles experience delays beyond the standard timeline, primarily due to incomplete documentation or valuation disputes.

Age Restrictions and Vehicle Standards for Kenya Imports

Kenya maintains strict age restrictions for vehicle imports, allowing only vehicles manufactured within the last 8 years for general imports. This restriction, implemented to reduce environmental impact and improve road safety, applies to all vehicle categories except commercial trucks and specialized equipment.

The 8-year age limit is calculated from the year of first registration in the country of origin. For example, a vehicle first registered in 2019 becomes ineligible for import to Kenya starting January 1, 2027. This rolling restriction ensures a constant supply of relatively modern vehicles in the Kenyan market.

Environmental and Safety Standards

All imported vehicles must meet Euro 4 emission standards minimum, with Euro 5 standards becoming mandatory for vehicles manufactured after 2025. KEBS conducts emission testing as part of the PVoC inspection process, and vehicles failing these tests cannot receive clearance certificates.

Right-hand drive configuration is mandatory for all vehicles imported to Kenya. Left-hand drive vehicles are strictly prohibited except for specific diplomatic or specialized applications with advance authorization from the Ministry of Transport. This requirement aligns with Kenya's colonial-era traffic patterns and regional East African standards.

Cost Analysis: Total Import Expenses for Used Cars

Understanding the complete cost structure helps importers budget accurately and avoid unexpected expenses. Beyond purchase price and duties, several additional costs significantly impact the total investment required for importing a used car to Kenya.

Breakdown of All Import-Related Costs

The total cost of importing a used car typically exceeds the initial purchase price by 80-120%, depending on vehicle value and shipping route. This comprehensive cost analysis covers all mandatory expenses from purchase to NTSA registration completion.

Cost Component Typical Range (USD) Percentage of Vehicle Value
Purchase Price 5,000-25,000 100%
Shipping & Insurance 800-1,500 8-15%
KRA Duties & Taxes 3,000-20,000 60-80%
Port Clearance 300-600 3-6%
NTSA Registration 80-150 1-2%
Transport to Destination 100-400 2-4%

Hidden Costs and Additional Expenses

Several expenses often catch first-time importers by surprise. Demurrage charges at Mombasa port accrue at USD 25-50 per day after the free storage period expires. Currency fluctuation between purchase and duty payment can add 3-7% to total costs, especially for transactions involving Japanese Yen or Euro.

Insurance requirements extend beyond shipping coverage. NTSA mandates comprehensive insurance before registration, with annual premiums ranging from 2-4% of vehicle value. Additionally, some vehicles require modification to meet local standards, such as installing speed governors or adjusting headlight patterns.

Documentation and Paperwork Requirements

Proper documentation prevents clearance delays and ensures smooth progression through each import stage. The Kenya Trade Portal estimates that 30% of import delays result from incomplete or incorrect documentation, making attention to detail critical for successful imports.

Essential Documents Checklist

Each document serves a specific purpose in the import process, and substitutions are generally not accepted by Kenyan authorities. Importers should verify document authenticity and completeness before initiating shipment to avoid costly delays at destination.

  • Export Certificate: Issued by country of origin, confirms legal export
  • Commercial Invoice: Must show accurate purchase price and payment terms
  • Bill of Lading: Original copy required, serves as title document
  • Insurance Certificate: Marine cargo insurance covering full CIF value
  • PVoC Certificate: Pre-shipment inspection confirming compliance
  • Manufacturer Certificate: Confirms production date and specifications
  • De-registration Certificate: Proves vehicle was properly de-registered at origin

Digital Documentation Trends

Kenya has embraced digital documentation through the Kenya TradeNet System, which accepts electronic copies for many documents. However, original physical documents remain mandatory for final customs clearance. The system allows importers to track processing status and receive updates on documentation requirements in real-time.

Blockchain-based verification is being piloted for vehicle import documentation, with full implementation expected by late 2026. This technology will reduce fraud and streamline verification processes between international shipping partners and Kenyan authorities.

Vehicle preparation at our German facilities includes compliance modifications such as right-hand drive confirmation, emission system verification, and safety equipment checks. This preparation reduces the risk of rejection during KEBS inspection and ensures smooth customs clearance.

Timeline Planning for Vehicle Import Process

Successful vehicle imports require careful timeline planning to coordinate multiple processes and minimize costs. The complete timeline from purchase to NTSA registration typically spans 45-60 days, depending on shipping route and documentation completeness.

Critical Timeline Milestones

Each milestone has dependencies that can affect the overall timeline. Planning buffer time for potential delays helps importers avoid rushed decisions or expedited service fees.

  1. Week 1-2: Vehicle purchase and export documentation preparation
  2. Week 3-4: PVoC inspection scheduling and completion
  3. Week 5-6: Shipping arrangement and vessel loading
  4. Week 7-8: Ocean transit (varies by route and shipping line)
  5. Week 9-10: Mombasa port clearance and customs processing
  6. Week 11-12: Transport to final destination and NTSA registration

Seasonal Considerations

Import timing affects both costs and processing speed. The December-January period sees increased volume due to holiday purchases, potentially extending clearance times by 2-3 days. Similarly, the March-April period coincides with financial year-end processing, which can slow government agency responses.

Weather patterns also impact shipping schedules. The monsoon season (April-June and October-December) can cause minor delays in vessel schedules, particularly for services originating from Japanese ports. Planning imports outside these peak periods often results in smoother processing and lower shipping rates.

faqItems.question: How much does it cost to import a used car to Kenya in 2026?
faqItems.answer: Total import costs typically range from 80-120% of the vehicle's purchase price. This includes KRA duties (60-85% of CIF value), shipping costs ($800-1,500), port clearance fees ($300-600), and NTSA registration ($80-150). For a $10,000 vehicle, expect total costs of $18,000-22,000.

faqItems.question: What is the maximum age for importing a used car to Kenya?
faqItems.answer: Kenya allows imports of vehicles up to 8 years old from the date of first registration. This is a rolling restriction, so a vehicle first registered in 2019 becomes ineligible for import starting January 1, 2027. Commercial trucks and specialized equipment may have different age limits.

faqItems.question: How long does NTSA registration take for imported vehicles?
faqItems.answer: NTSA registration typically takes 3-5 working days when all documentation is complete. Vehicles over 8 years old or those requiring physical inspection may take up to 10 working days. Registration must be completed within 14 calendar days of customs clearance to avoid penalties.

faqItems.question: Can I track my vehicle clearance status at Mombasa port?
faqItems.answer: Yes, you can track clearance status through the Kenya TradeNet System using your import declaration number. The system provides real-time updates on documentation processing, customs examination, and clearance approval. Most clearing agents also provide regular status updates to their clients.

faqItems.question: What happens if my imported vehicle fails KEBS inspection?
faqItems.answer: Vehicles failing KEBS inspection cannot be cleared for import and may face re-exportation or destruction at the importer's expense. Common failure reasons include emission standard non-compliance, safety equipment defects, or age restriction violations. Pre-export verification through authorized agents helps prevent such failures.

tldr: Importing a used car to Kenya in 2026 requires KRA duty payments of 60-85% of vehicle value, NTSA registration within 14 days of clearance, and typically 7-10 working days for Mombasa port processing. Proper documentation and understanding age restrictions (8 years maximum) are critical for successful imports.
